summary: The paper proposes CDAS, a steering method combining a JSD-based distribution-matching objective with Distributed Interchange Interventions (DII) inspired by DAS, aimed at more faithful bi-directional model control. The conceptual contribution — reframing steering as a causal-variable-localization-adjacent problem rather than preference optimization — is interesting and well-motivated, and the safety-focused case studies (refusal override, CoT backdoor) provide useful evidence that CDAS preserves utility better than RePS on larger models. However, the AXBench evidence is mixed (CDAS underperforms RePS/Lang. on Gemma-2-2B and at layer 31 on 9B, and requires factor tuning that undermines the paper's tuning-free framing), variance/seed reporting is inconsistent, and the case studies rely on small numbers of models (3 for refusal, a single self-trained backdoor model), which limits the generality claims.
strengths: Genuinely new training objective: using JSD between intervened and counterfactual output distributions is a meaningful conceptual departure from Lang./PO objectives, and the connection to DAS/DII is well argued.
Honest, well-scoped framing: the authors explicitly state CDAS is not always better than strong-supervised methods, position it as complementary, and clearly enumerate limitations.

Two safety-relevant case studies (refusal override, CoT backdoor) go beyond benchmark chasing and give the method meaningful stress tests, with utility preservation evidence via MMLU/TruthfulQA/tinyBenchmarks and KL divergence.
Bi-directional formulation is natural in the objective (D+ and D- terms) and mirrors what BiPO/RePS achieve with contrastive losses.
KL-divergence-to-natural-distribution as a faithfulness metric complements task metrics and shows CDAS's most consistent advantage.

key_concerns.issue: AXBench results (Table 1) do not clearly support the main claim of advancing general-purpose steering: CDAS with 'fair' factor selection is beaten by RePS on 3 of 4 setups, and even the highlighted 9B/L20 win depends on tuned factors while the 'unit factor' variant (the principled setting) is dramatically weaker across the board. The paper's narrative that CDAS is 'more consistent across layers' rests on one 2B comparison and hides the collapse at 9B/L31.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report seed variance / confidence intervals on Table 1, add more intervening layers (not just two per model) to substantiate the consistency claim, and either drop or clearly downgrade the general-purpose-steering framing to reflect that CDAS is layer-sensitive and factor-tuning-sensitive.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical soundness is uneven. Table 1 reports no error bars or seeds; Table 2 refusal/suppression scores show no variance; Table 4 uses only 100 examples per benchmark. Only Figure 1 shows standard error. Some differences the paper draws conclusions from (e.g., 'CDAS is most faithful') are small and could be within noise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean ± std over ≥3 seeds for every table, include statistical tests (paired bootstrap or sign test) for head-to-head claims vs RePS/DAS, and add full-size benchmark evaluation for at least the refusal case study.

key_concerns.issue: The backdoor case study rests on a single self-trained poisoned model and hand-plus-LLM-augmented red-teaming set (n=272). ASR@L16 = 6.68% on the true trigger is claimed as the strongest neutralization result, but with a single model and one trigger, generalization to other backdoor designs, triggers, or base models is unsupported.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Train at least 2–3 backdoor variants (different triggers, different base models, or the Anthropic sleeper-agent recipe with variations) and report ASR distributions. Alternatively, scope the claim explicitly to this one instantiation.

key_concerns.issue: The 'tuning-free advantage' is inconsistently applied. Section 4 shows CDAS needs β>1 grid search to compete on AXBench, while Sections 5.1–5.2 use unit factors and highlight tuning-free operation. The paper does not clearly explain when/why unit factors suffice, weakening the practical guidance.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide an analysis (e.g., relating training-set concept-eliciting instruction strength or activation magnitudes to whether β=1 suffices), and quantify sensitivity of results to β across settings.

key_concerns.issue: Related-work positioning against DAS is fair but the 'CDAS is not causal variable localization' caveat undercuts the mechanistic-interpretability framing used to motivate the method; the paper simultaneously leans on and disowns the DAS grounding.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Tighten the theoretical framing — either commit to a causal-abstraction interpretation with a concrete claim tested empirically, or rebrand as an inspired-by-DAS engineering method and adjust the introduction/conclusion accordingly.

key_concerns.issue: Prose has numerous awkward, run-on sentences and comma splices (likely from formatting), and Table 2 as extracted is partially garbled (rows misaligned). Even acknowledging PDF extraction, some passages in the body (e.g., the intuition paragraph in 3.3) would benefit from tightening.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Copy-edit the manuscript; ensure Table 2 renders cleanly with clearly delimited columns; break long sentences in Sections 1 and 5.

key_concerns.issue: The 'one-to-many' DII intervention location (a single token in the <model> template) is chosen via grid search, but the paper does not report sensitivity to this choice or discuss failure modes when the chat template differs.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add an ablation over source-token position and discuss transfer to models with different chat templates.

questions_for_authors: Can you show CDAS results across more layers (e.g., every 4 layers) on both Gemma-2 models to substantiate the 'more consistent across layers' claim?
What is the seed-to-seed variance of the AXBench and refusal-suppression numbers? Are the CDAS-vs-RePS differences on Llama-3.1-70B statistically significant?

For the backdoor study, does CDAS transfer if you train the backdoor on a different base model (e.g., Gemma) or with a different trigger? A single poisoned model makes the neutralization claim hard to generalize.
How sensitive are Section 5 results to the choice of unit-factor αc? What if you compute αc from a different subset of Dctrain?

The intuition contrasts 'faithfully identifying concept features' with 'imposing external policies,' but at inference you still clamp to a scaled subspace. In what sense is the deployed intervention 'faithful' beyond having lower KL divergence than PO baselines?
Why is BiPO excluded from the case studies? Excluding a baseline because it underperforms on a different benchmark risks a self-serving comparison.
calibration_check: Claims are mostly appropriately scoped — the authors explicitly concede CDAS 'may not always outperform' and position it as complementary — but the phrase 'advances the performance frontier on Gemma-2-9B' overreaches given that CDAS only wins one of two 9B layers and depends on tuned factors.

significance.justification: Introduces a plausible new axis (distribution matching for steering) but the empirical case for practical impact is mixed; likely of interest to the steering/interpretability subcommunity rather than practice-changing.

novelty.justification: The JSD-matching objective combined with DII-based bi-directional steering is a genuine conceptual contribution not present in Lang./BiPO/RePS, even though it builds heavily on DAS.

rigor.justification: Method is coherent and controls are reasonable, but conclusions about consistency/faithfulness sometimes generalize beyond the tested layers, seeds, and models.

statistical_soundness.justification: Most tables lack error bars or seed information; only Figure 1 reports standard error, and several claims of superiority are made over small margins without significance tests.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper is refreshingly candid about CDAS not always winning and enumerates concrete limitations, though the 'advances the frontier' phrasing on 9B is a mild overreach.

clarity.justification: The method is precisely specified in equations, but the prose is uneven with long run-ons, and the interplay between unit-factor vs tuned-factor settings across sections is confusing.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference structure (intro, related work, method, benchmark, case studies, conclusion) is followed, and length appears within ICLR norms.

reproducibility.justification: Objective, DII protocol, training data curation, and hyperparameter strategies are described sufficiently in principle; some case-study details rely on appendices and the augmentation prompts, but reproducing given data/checkpoints appears feasible.

related_work.justification: Positions the work against DAS, BiPO, RePS, DIM, LoReFT, refusal-direction and backdoor-probing literature; positioning is fair though the causal-abstraction claim is later softened by the 'CDAS is not causal variable localization' caveat.

figure_quality.justification: Table captions and Figure 1 are informative and directly tied to claims; however, Table 1 and Table 2 encode a lot of numbers without variance and the extracted Table 2 layout suggests dense presentation that could obscure comparisons.

breadth_generality.justification: Two Gemma sizes on AXBench plus three safety models and a single self-trained backdoor is reasonable coverage, but each individual setting has narrow support (few layers, few models per case study), making the 'benefits from scale' claim under-supported.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject: interesting, novel objective with honest framing and useful case studies, but mixed AXBench results, thin statistical rigor, and single-instance backdoor evaluation keep it below the ICLR acceptance bar as submitted.
